content: Breast milk is universally acknowledged as the optimal source of nutrition for infants. However, the effect of antenatal breastfeeding education on the duration of breastfeeding has not been thoroughly evaluated. This study aimed to assess whether antenatal breastfeeding education improves breastfeeding initiation and duration. To conduct this review, a comprehensive search was performed across multiple databases, including Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth's Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and Scopus, up to March 1, 2016. Experts were contacted, and reference lists of relevant articles were reviewed. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated the impact of formal antenatal breastfeeding education or compared different methods of such education on breastfeeding duration. Trials that combined antenatal education with intrapartum or postpartum components were excluded. Cluster-randomized trials were included, but quasi-randomized trials were not eligible. Data from the included studies were extracted by two reviewers, and discrepancies were resolved through discussion. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. A total of 24 studies involving 10,056 women were included in this review, with 20 studies (9,789 women) contributing data to the analyses. Most of these studies were conducted in high-income countries, such as the USA, UK, Canada, and Australia. For the first five comparisons, data were presented according to the type of intervention without pooling results. Cluster-randomized trials reported adjusted odds ratios (ORs), and the generic inverse variance method was used for analysis. However, the use of ORs prevented the pooling of these trials in the main analyses. When comparing one method of breastfeeding education with standard care, no significant differences were observed in the duration of breastfeeding (measured in days or weeks). There was no evidence that these interventions improved the proportion of women engaging in any breastfeeding or exclusive breastfeeding at three or six months. Single trials of various interventions did not demonstrate significant improvements in breastfeeding initiation, except for one small trial with a high risk of attrition bias. While some results slightly favored the intervention, the confidence intervals were wide and crossed the line of no effect. Breastfeeding complications, such as mastitis, were similar between intervention and control groups in the trials that reported these outcomes. When multiple methods of breastfeeding education were compared to standard care, one three-arm study found that a combination of a breastfeeding booklet, video, and lactation consultant significantly improved the proportion of women exclusively breastfeeding at three months (OR 2.60, 95% CI 1.25 to 5.40) and marginally at six months (OR 2.40, 95% CI 1.00 to 5.76). However, the same study found that an intervention without a lactation consultant (using only the booklet and video) did not yield similar improvements. Another study reported that monthly breastfeeding sessions combined with weekly cell phone messages improved exclusive breastfeeding rates at both three months (OR 1.80, 95% CI 1.10 to 2.95) and six months (OR 2.40, 95% CI 1.40 to 4.11). This intervention also improved breastfeeding initiation rates (OR 2.61, 95% CI 1.61 to 4.24). For pooled analyses in the Summary of Findings table, cluster-randomized trials were excluded. The evidence did not show that antenatal breastfeeding education improved exclusive breastfeeding rates at three months (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.25) or six months (RR 1.07, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.30). Similarly, there were no significant differences in the proportion of women engaging in any breastfeeding at three months (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.18) or six months (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.23). There was also no evidence that antenatal breastfeeding education improved breastfeeding initiation rates (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.09). The quality of evidence was downgraded in some cases due to small sample sizes or wide confidence intervals. In conclusion, there is no definitive evidence that antenatal breastfeeding education improves breastfeeding initiation, the proportion of women breastfeeding (either exclusively or at all) at three or six months, or the overall duration of breastfeeding. High-quality randomized controlled trials are urgently needed to evaluate the effectiveness and potential adverse effects of antenatal breastfeeding education, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. The findings of this review are primarily applicable to high-income settings.
